name: Short Choke from Harness
description: Learn the Short Choke from Harness in BJJ. Master gi lapel choke mechanics, grip threading sequences, and finishing details from seatbelt back control.
overview:
The Short Choke from Harness is a gi-specific blood choke executed from back control with seatbelt grip. The attacker threads the choking arm across the opponent's neck and feeds the hand into their own opposite sleeve, creating a compact compression mechanism against the carotid arteries. Unlike the Rear Naked Choke, which requires threading the arm fully behind the head, the Short Choke uses the gi sleeve as an anchor point, making it effective even when the opponent maintains a strong chin tuck defense.

This submission is particularly valuable when the opponent defends the traditional RNC by keeping their chin buried and both hands fighting the choking arm. The Short Choke bypasses this defense because the sleeve grip creates a shorter lever that can compress the neck without needing to get behind the chin. The choking pressure comes from the forearm driving across the throat while the sleeve connection prevents the arm from being stripped, creating a tight loop around the neck.

From the Harness position specifically, the seatbelt grip provides the ideal starting configuration. The over-arm is already positioned near the neck, and the transition to the Short Choke requires minimal positional adjustment. The attacker maintains chest-to-back connection and hook control throughout, making this a low-risk, high-reward attack that preserves back control even if the finish is unsuccessful.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to loss of consciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential for confusion lasting 30-60 seconds

injury_risks.injury: Trachea compression if technique is misapplied
injury_risks.recovery_time: 1-3 days of throat soreness; seek medical attention if breathing difficulty persists

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on partner or mat
Any distress signal including body going limp
release_protocol: Immediately release lapel grip and remove all pressure from neck
Remove your weight from opponent's torso to allow breathing
Check partner's consciousness and breathing status
If partner is unconscious, elevate legs and monitor airway
Never apply the choke again in the same training session if unconsciousness occurred
training_restrictions: Never apply sudden jerking motions with the lapel
Never continue pressure after tap signal
Never practice on partners with neck injuries or medical conditions
Always ensure partner can tap with at least one hand
Never use competition speed during initial learning phases

attacker.name: from Harness Attacker
attacker.description: Master attacking the Short Choke from Harness in BJJ. Step-by-step grip threading, sleeve mechanics, and finishing sequences from seatbelt back control.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the Short Choke from Harness requires precise grip threading and timing. The seatbelt position provides the ideal launching platform, with the over-arm already positioned near the opponent's neck. The key mechanical advantage lies in using your gi sleeve as an anchor point, creating a compact choking loop that bypasses the opponent's chin tuck defense. Success depends on maintaining chest-to-back connection throughout the attack while systematically removing the opponent's hand fighting grips to thread the choking arm into position.
key_principles: Maintain chest-to-back pressure throughout the entire attack sequence to prevent opponent from creating escape space
Use the gi sleeve as a force multiplier - the fabric creates friction that prevents grip slippage and amplifies choking pressure
Thread the choking arm progressively rather than forcing it across in one motion, using small incremental advances
Keep hooks active and engaged during the choke attempt to prevent opponent from turning or hip escaping
Control the opponent's defensive hand before committing to the choke - two-on-one their fighting hand momentarily to create a window
Apply the choke by driving the forearm blade across the neck while pulling the sleeve connection tight, creating bilateral carotid compression
setup_requirements: Established seatbelt grip with over-arm positioned on the choking side near opponent's neck
At least one hook inserted to prevent opponent from turning or escaping during the choke attempt
Opponent's defensive hands occupied or temporarily controlled to allow arm threading across the neck
Chest-to-back connection maintained with forward pressure to limit opponent's mobility
Gi sleeve accessible on the under-arm side for the anchor grip insertion

execution_steps.description: From the seatbelt grip, adjust your over-arm so the forearm is positioned high across the opponent's chest near the collarbone. Your hand should be on the choking side, ready to thread across the neck. Maintain strong chest pressure to keep the opponent flat and limit their defensive hand fighting ability.

Use your under-arm to momentarily trap or redirect the opponent's primary defensive hand. Pull their defending wrist toward their hip with your under-arm, or use your chest pressure to pin their arm against their body. This creates the brief window needed to advance the choking arm without resistance.

execution_steps.action: Thread the choking arm across the neck
execution_steps.description: With the defensive hand controlled, slide your forearm blade across the opponent's throat, positioning the radius bone directly against the near-side carotid artery. Keep your elbow tight to your body and do not flare it outward, as this creates space for the opponent to insert their chin or hand to block the advance.

Once the forearm is across the neck, insert your choking hand into the opening of your opposite gi sleeve near the wrist or mid-forearm area. Grip the inside of the sleeve fabric firmly with your fingers. This creates the short anchor that prevents the opponent from stripping the choking arm and locks the forearm in position across the neck.

execution_steps.action: Secure the connection and close gaps
execution_steps.description: Pull your sleeve-gripping hand slightly back while driving the choking forearm forward into the neck. Your under-arm should come up to support the back of the opponent's head or grip your own bicep to create additional structural reinforcement. Squeeze your elbows together to tighten the loop around the neck and eliminate any remaining gaps.

Complete the choke by expanding your chest against their back while simultaneously squeezing your arms together. Arch slightly backward to increase the pressure on both carotid arteries. The finish should feel like you are trying to touch your own elbows together behind their neck. Maintain hook control throughout to prevent any last-moment escape attempts.

common_counters.counter: Opponent strips the choking arm with two-on-one grip before sleeve connection is established
common_counters.your_response: Re-establish seatbelt grip and use incremental threading. Control their fighting hand with your under-arm momentarily before each advance rather than forcing the arm across in one motion.

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin and frames with both hands on the choking forearm to block advancement
common_counters.your_response: Use your under-arm to peel one defensive hand away while maintaining forearm pressure. Adjust the angle of your forearm to slide above the jaw line, using the bony edge to wedge the chin up and create space to thread underneath.

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns into you by rotating toward the under-hook side and recovers guard
common_counters.your_response: Drive hooks deeper and increase chest pressure to prevent rotation. If they commit to the turn, switch to a guillotine or arm triangle setup that capitalizes on their exposed neck during the rotation rather than fighting their momentum.

common_counters.counter: Opponent grabs your sleeve opening before you can feed your hand into it
common_counters.your_response: Break their one-handed grip on the fabric by pulling sharply or adjusting to feed from a different angle. A single hand gripping a sleeve opening is a weak control point that can be cleared with a quick wrist rotation or by switching to the other sleeve.

common_errors.error: Forcing the arm across the neck in one aggressive motion
common_errors.consequence: Opponent times the movement and inserts both hands to block, or uses the momentum to initiate an escape by turning into the gap created
common_errors.correction: Thread the arm incrementally with small advances, controlling one defensive hand at a time before each progression

common_errors.error: Releasing chest-to-back pressure while setting up the choke
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for opponent to turn, hip escape, or establish defensive frames that prevent the choke from being completed
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant forward pressure through your torso throughout the entire setup, using hooks to anchor your position

common_errors.error: Gripping the outside of the sleeve instead of threading the hand inside
common_errors.consequence: The grip is weaker, can be stripped more easily, and the choking angle becomes less effective without the sleeve acting as a true structural anchor
common_errors.correction: Insert the hand fully into the sleeve opening and grip the internal fabric for a secure connection that resists stripping attempts

common_errors.error: Neglecting hook control during the choke attempt
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses the momentary focus on upper body to clear hooks and escape to turtle or guard, losing the dominant back position entirely
common_errors.correction: Keep hooks actively engaged with heels pulling toward your hips throughout the choke setup and finish sequence

common_errors.error: Attempting the Short Choke before controlling the opponent's defensive hands
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily strips the choking arm with both free hands, wasting energy and potentially exposing the attacking arm to a two-on-one grip break
common_errors.correction: Always address the primary defensive hand with your under-arm before committing the choking arm across the neck

common_errors.error: Squeezing only with the arms instead of incorporating chest expansion and body mechanics
common_errors.consequence: The choke relies solely on arm strength, leading to rapid fatigue and insufficient pressure to compress both carotid arteries for the finish
common_errors.correction: Finish by expanding your chest against their back while squeezing arms together, using the large muscles of your torso for the primary choking force

training_progressions.description: Practice the arm threading sequence on a cooperative partner. Focus on smooth forearm placement across the neck, finding the sleeve opening, and securing the internal grip. Repeat 20-30 times per side with no resistance to build the motor pattern.

training_progressions.focus: Combining grip threading with positional maintenance
training_progressions.description: From full harness position, practice the complete setup sequence including defensive hand control, arm threading, and sleeve grip. Partner provides light hand fighting resistance but does not attempt full escapes. Focus on maintaining chest contact throughout.

training_progressions.focus: Completing the choke against increasing defense
training_progressions.description: Partner provides graduated defensive resistance at 30%, 50%, then 70% intensity. Practice overcoming chin tucks, hand fighting, and frame attempts. Emphasize maintaining back control even when the choke attempt fails.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance application integrated into back attack system
training_progressions.description: Start from established harness position in live positional sparring rounds. Integrate the Short Choke into your overall back attack system alongside RNC, bow and arrow, and armbar options. Focus on recognizing the right moment to initiate the choke versus pursuing alternative attacks.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Short Choke from Harness primarily target?
flashcards.answer: The Short Choke targets the carotid arteries on both sides of the neck through bilateral compression. The forearm blade compresses the near-side carotid artery while the gi sleeve connection creates pressure on the far-side carotid. This is a blood choke that restricts blood flow to the brain rather than compressing the airway, which is why it can cause unconsciousness within seconds when properly applied.

flashcards.question: Your opponent has their chin tucked tightly with both hands defending the choking arm - what adjustment allows you to complete the choke?
flashcards.answer: Use your under-arm to momentarily trap one defensive hand by pulling it toward their hip, creating a brief window. Then thread your forearm above their chin defense, targeting the jaw line to wedge the chin up. The sleeve anchor means you do not need full arm penetration behind the chin like an RNC. The short choke compresses the carotids even with the chin partially tucked because the forearm angle and sleeve leverage are different from a traditional strangle.

flashcards.question: What are the key indicators that the choke is properly set and the opponent is close to tapping?
flashcards.answer: The opponent's hand fighting becomes weaker or more frantic, their breathing changes to rapid gasping, and their body may begin to stiffen or go slack. The forearm should feel locked against the neck with no gaps between the radius bone and the carotid. When you squeeze, you should feel bilateral pressure through both the forearm and sleeve connection. If the opponent's face changes color or they stop resisting entirely, be prepared for an immediate tap or loss of consciousness and apply pressure slowly.

flashcards.question: What control elements must be established before committing to the Short Choke from Harness?
flashcards.answer: You need an established seatbelt grip with the over-arm on the choking side positioned near the neck, at least one hook inserted for lower body control, maintained chest-to-back pressure with no space between torsos, and the opponent's primary defensive hand either controlled or momentarily redirected. Attempting the choke without these prerequisites significantly reduces the success rate and risks losing the dominant four-point back position.

flashcards.question: What is the point of no escape once the Short Choke is locked in?
flashcards.answer: Once the forearm is threaded across the neck and the hand is inserted into the opposite sleeve with a secure internal grip, escape options drop dramatically. Stripping the choking arm now requires overcoming both the forearm pressure and the fabric anchor simultaneously, which is extremely difficult with one hand. The choke becomes nearly inescapable once the attacker begins squeezing with both arms and expanding the chest, as bilateral carotid compression causes rapid blood flow restriction to the brain.

flashcards.question: How do you adjust your grip when the opponent keeps stripping your choking forearm before you reach the sleeve?
flashcards.answer: Switch to an incremental approach by using your under-arm to create a two-on-one on their primary defensive wrist, pulling it toward their hip. Then advance the choking forearm a few inches at a time rather than threading it across in one motion. If they consistently strip with both hands, feint the choke to draw their hands high, then switch to an armbar setup on the exposed arm. Return to the choke when their defensive hands reposition to address the armbar threat.

flashcards.question: What are the critical safety considerations when applying the Short Choke in training?
flashcards.answer: Apply the choke slowly over 3-5 seconds minimum in training, giving your partner adequate time to recognize the pressure and tap. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness in as little as 4-6 seconds when fully locked, so never apply sudden explosive pressure. Release immediately upon any tap signal including verbal taps, hand taps, or foot taps on the mat. Monitor your partner for signs of unconsciousness such as going limp, and if they lose consciousness, release immediately, elevate their legs, and monitor their airway until they recover.

flashcards.question: How should you release the Short Choke after your partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release the sleeve grip and remove the forearm from the neck in one smooth motion. Remove your chest pressure from their back to allow unrestricted breathing. Do not maintain aggressive hook pressure during the release phase. Check that your partner is conscious and responsive before continuing. If they show any signs of confusion or disorientation, give them time to fully recover. Never re-apply the choke in the same round if there was any indication of loss of consciousness.

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts to posture up and create space between their back and your chest - what adjustment prevents the escape?
flashcards.answer: Drive your hips forward and increase downward pressure through your hooks to prevent them from sitting upright. Simultaneously tighten the seatbelt grip and pull them back into your chest. If they have already created significant space, abort the choke attempt and focus on re-establishing tight chest-to-back connection before trying again. Attempting to finish the choke with space between bodies reduces effectiveness dramatically and risks losing the position entirely.

flashcards.question: In competition, what strategic factors affect when to attempt the Short Choke versus other back attacks?
flashcards.answer: The Short Choke is most effective when the opponent commits to RNC defense with both hands high and chin tucked, as the sleeve grip bypasses this specific defense. Attempt it when their defensive hands are occupied fighting your choking arm rather than maintaining positional frames. In competition the gi often becomes sweaty, so confirm the sleeve opening is accessible and dry enough for a secure grip. If you are ahead on points, prioritize maintaining back control points rather than risking the position on a speculative choke attempt.

defender.name: from Harness Defender
defender.description: Learn to defend and escape the Short Choke from Harness in BJJ. Recognition cues, hand fighting sequences, and escape paths from back control.
defender.overview: Defending the Short Choke from Harness requires early recognition and systematic hand fighting to prevent the forearm from threading across the neck. The most critical defensive window occurs before the opponent secures their hand in the sleeve, as this anchor point makes the choke extremely difficult to strip. Defenders must prioritize two-on-one control of the choking arm, maintain a strong chin tuck, and create frames that prevent the forearm from advancing. When prevention fails, the defender must immediately address the sleeve grip before full compression is applied, using rotation and hip movement to create escape angles.
key_principles: Recognize the choke setup early by monitoring the over-arm position and any hand movement toward the opposite sleeve opening
Maintain two-on-one control on the choking arm at all times, prioritizing wrist and forearm grips that prevent threading across the neck
Keep chin tucked firmly to chest to create a physical barrier against the forearm crossing the neck
Address the sleeve grip immediately if established - once locked in the sleeve, the choke becomes exponentially harder to defend
Create defensive frames by positioning elbows tight to the body and using shoulder pressure to close gaps around the neck
Turn toward the under-hook side when escaping to disrupt the choking angle and create maximum distance from the choking arm
recognition_cues: Opponent's over-arm begins sliding higher from the chest position toward the neck or collarbone area, indicating they are preparing to thread across
Opponent's under-arm temporarily releases the seatbelt configuration to control or redirect your primary defensive hand downward
Opponent adjusts their body angle or posture to bring the choking arm sleeve closer to their opposite hand for the feed
Opponent increases forward chest pressure and tightens hooks simultaneously, indicating they are stabilizing before an offensive attack sequence

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one grip on choking forearm to prevent threading across the neck
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as the over-arm begins moving from the chest toward the neck area, before the forearm crosses the throat
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the choke from being established and returns to standard defensive hand fighting from harness bottom
defensive_options.risk: Both hands committed to one arm temporarily exposes the other side to alternative attacks like armbar setups

defensive_options.action: Strip the sleeve grip by peeling fingers from the fabric before the choke tightens
defensive_options.when_to_use: After the opponent has threaded the forearm across but before they fully insert and secure their hand inside the sleeve opening
defensive_options.if_successful: Removes the structural anchor and forces the opponent to restart the entire choke setup sequence from scratch
defensive_options.risk: Requires releasing two-on-one forearm control momentarily to reach the sleeve connection point

defensive_options.action: Turn toward the under-hook side while hip escaping to recover guard position
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the choking arm is partially across but not yet locked with the sleeve grip, and you have enough hip mobility to initiate rotation
defensive_options.if_successful: Escapes back control entirely and recovers to a neutral guard position where the choke threat is eliminated
defensive_options.risk: Incomplete rotation may allow the opponent to secure a deeper choke or follow the turn to maintain back control

defensive_options.action: Hip escape and clear hooks to create distance and disrupt the choking angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the opponent temporarily loosens hooks or shifts weight distribution upward to set up the choke threading
defensive_options.if_successful: Creates space that disrupts the choke angle and may allow progression to full escape via turtle or half guard
defensive_options.risk: Moving hips away can sometimes make hook re-insertion easier if the timing of the escape is poor

escape_paths: Strip the choking arm with two-on-one grip control, then turn toward the under-hook side while hip escaping to recover closed guard or half guard
Clear the bottom hook by pushing with your same-side foot, hip escape to create an angle, then turtle and work toward standing or guard recovery
If the choke is partially locked, tuck chin aggressively while peeling the sleeve grip with both hands, then immediately rotate away from the choking side to escape to turtle position

favorable_outcomes.how: Successfully strip the choking arm using two-on-one control and rotate toward the under-hook side, using hip movement and momentum to turn fully and establish closed guard from the resulting scramble

common_errors.error: Attempting to escape the position before neutralizing the choking arm threat
common_errors.consequence: The choking arm slides freely across the neck during the escape movement, allowing the opponent to finish the choke while the defender is in a compromised defensive posture
common_errors.correction: Always neutralize the choking arm threat first with two-on-one grip control before initiating any positional escape sequence

common_errors.error: Using only one hand to fight the choking arm while reaching behind with the other for the opponent's head
common_errors.consequence: Leaves the choking arm insufficiently controlled with one hand, creating an opening for the forearm to advance across the neck and reach the sleeve
common_errors.correction: Commit both hands to the choking arm with a strong two-on-one grip until the immediate choke threat is fully neutralized

common_errors.error: Lifting the chin to look around or create space instead of keeping it buried against the chest
common_errors.consequence: Exposes the throat directly to the forearm blade and makes the choke significantly easier to complete by removing the primary physical barrier
common_errors.correction: Keep chin firmly tucked against the chest with the shoulder raised on the choking side to close all gaps around the neck

common_errors.error: Ignoring the sleeve grip once established and only fighting against the forearm pressure on the neck
common_errors.consequence: The sleeve anchor prevents the arm from being stripped even with strong two-handed fighting, allowing the choke to progressively tighten with each squeeze
common_errors.correction: If the hand reaches the sleeve, immediately redirect both hands to breaking the sleeve grip connection before attempting to address the forearm position on the neck

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the Short Choke from Harness is being set up versus a standard RNC attempt?
flashcards.answer: The key difference is the opponent's hand trajectory after the forearm crosses the neck. In an RNC setup, the choking arm threads behind your head toward the opposite shoulder to complete the figure-four lock. In the Short Choke, the choking hand moves toward the opponent's own opposite sleeve opening rather than behind your head. Watch for the opponent adjusting their gi sleeve position or moving their choking hand toward their own forearm. The defensive window closes once the hand enters the sleeve.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap when caught in the Short Choke from Harness?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately with your hand on the opponent's body, arm, or leg wherever you can make clear physical contact. If your hands are trapped or unable to reach, use a verbal tap by clearly saying tap or making any audible distress signal. You can also tap with your feet on the mat. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness in 4-6 seconds when fully locked, so never delay tapping to attempt a desperate last-second escape. Tapping early and resetting is always safer than risking loss of consciousness.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available against the Short Choke at different stages of completion?
flashcards.answer: Before the forearm crosses the neck: maintain two-on-one grip control on the choking arm and keep chin tucked to physically block threading. After the forearm crosses but before the sleeve grip: strip the forearm with both hands while turning toward the underhook side to escape. After the sleeve grip is established: target the sleeve connection itself with both hands to break the anchor before addressing the forearm. Once fully locked and tightening: tuck chin, make one attempt to peel the sleeve grip, and if pressure increases, tap immediately.

flashcards.question: Why is the sleeve grip the most critical element to prevent when defending the Short Choke?
flashcards.answer: The sleeve grip acts as a structural anchor that transforms the choking arm from a movable limb into a locked mechanism. Without the sleeve grip, the opponent must rely on arm strength alone to maintain forearm pressure, and a strong two-on-one defense can strip the arm away. With the sleeve grip secured, the fabric creates friction and structural reinforcement that makes stripping nearly impossible regardless of hand fighting effort. The choke can then be finished with minimal additional force, making prevention of the sleeve connection the single highest-priority defensive action.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying choke setup cues and maintaining defensive grip positions
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly sets up the Short Choke while the defender practices recognizing the arm movement patterns and maintaining two-on-one grip control. No resistance from the defender on escapes. Focus entirely on hand positioning, chin tuck timing, and identifying the moment the sleeve feed begins.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 2: Grip Stripping and Escape Timing
training_progressions.focus: Breaking the choke grip at each stage of completion
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes the choke to varying degrees of completion while the defender practices stripping at each stage: before crossing, after crossing but before sleeve insertion, and after sleeve grip is secured. Practice the turn and hip escape at each defensive checkpoint.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance defense and escape under pressure
training_progressions.description: Start from harness bottom against a partner actively attacking with the Short Choke at full intensity. Defend and escape under realistic resistance. Track success rates at each defensive stage to identify where your defense breaks down and focus future training on those specific checkpoints.
